items.prompt: What is a 'race condition'?
choices: A bug where the correctness of a result depends on the relative timing of two or more operations on shared state
Any bug that only happens under heavy server load
A deadlock between two threads waiting on each other
A memory leak caused by unreleased resources
items.explanation: A race condition is specifically about timing-dependent correctness — the same code can produce a right or wrong result depending on how two operations happen to interleave.
items.reference:
Race condition
⏱️ Correctness depends on timing
🔀 Result varies with interleaving
Why: the operations are each correct alone — the bug lives in the ordering.

items.prompt: Two buyers both purchase the last unit of stock successfully. What kind of bug is this?

A syntax error in the purchase function
A memory leak in the inventory store
An off-by-one error in the stock count logic
items.explanation: Both purchase requests ran individually-correct code; the bug only appears because of how their timing interleaved, which is the defining trait of a race condition.
items.reference:
Race condition
⏱️ Correctness depends on timing
🔀 Result varies with interleaving
Why: the operations are each correct alone — the bug lives in the ordering.

items.prompt: What is a 'critical section'?
choices: The span of code, from reading a shared value to finishing the update based on it, that must not be interrupted
Any function that takes longer than 100ms to execute
The part of a program that handles error logging
A section of code that only runs during server startup
items.explanation: The critical section is the read-to-write span where an interruption from another operation touching the same shared value would corrupt the result.
items.reference:
Critical section
📖 Read shared value
✍️ ... act on it ...
🚫 Must not be interrupted in between
Why: this span is exactly where a race condition can slip in.

items.prompt: In the oversold-item bug, which part of the code is the critical section?
choices: From reading the stock value to writing the decremented value back
Only the line that sends the 'purchase successful' response
The entire server process, from startup to shutdown
Only the initial stock value assignment when the server boots
items.explanation: The critical section is exactly the read-check-write span — that's where a second request's read can land in the gap before the first request's write.
items.reference:
Critical section
📖 Read shared value
✍️ ... act on it ...
🚫 Must not be interrupted in between
Why: this span is exactly where a race condition can slip in.

items.prompt: What does 'atomicity' guarantee about an operation?
choices: It happens as a single, indivisible step — nothing else can observe it half-done
It always completes in under 1 millisecond
It never fails or throws an error
It runs on a dedicated CPU core
items.explanation: Atomicity is about indivisibility from other operations' point of view, not about speed or reliability — an atomic operation can still fail, it just can't be observed partially done.
items.reference:
Atomicity
🧱 Indivisible from outside
🚫 No 'half-done' observable state
Why: atomicity closes the gap a race condition exploits, by removing the gap entirely.

items.prompt: Why does making the check-and-decrement atomic fix the oversold-item bug?
choices: Because no other request can read the value mid-operation once the check and update are one indivisible step
Because atomic operations are always faster than non-atomic ones
Because atomicity automatically retries failed purchases
Because atomic operations can't be canceled by the user
items.explanation: The bug exists because another request can read the shared value between the check and the write — atomicity removes that window entirely, not by speeding anything up.
items.reference:
Atomicity
🧱 Indivisible from outside
🚫 No 'half-done' observable state
Why: atomicity closes the gap a race condition exploits, by removing the gap entirely.

items.prompt: What does a lock (mutex) do?
choices: Lets only one operation enter a critical section at a time, forcing others to wait their turn
Prevents a program from crashing on invalid input
Encrypts shared data so other processes can't read it
Automatically retries a failed operation until it succeeds
items.explanation: A lock's job is serialization: it makes concurrent callers wait outside the critical section instead of interleaving into it.
items.reference:
Lock (mutex)
🔒 One caller in the critical section
⏳ Others wait their turn
Why: a lock fixes races by serializing access, not by removing the gap.

items.prompt: Why might a lock be preferred over an atomic operation for a given critical section?
choices: When the critical section spans multiple resources or an operation that can't be expressed as one atomic step
When the critical section is very short and simple
When the shared data never changes
When performance is the single highest priority
items.explanation: Locks are more general than atomic operations — they work no matter how complex the critical section is, which matters when a single atomic primitive can't express the whole operation.
items.reference:
Lock (mutex)
🔒 One caller in the critical section
⏳ Others wait their turn
Why: a lock fixes races by serializing access, not by removing the gap.

items.prompt: What does TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) refer to?
choices: The gap between reading a shared value and acting on it, where another operation can read the same stale value
The total time a server takes to respond to a request
A timeout error that occurs when a database query takes too long
The time between when code is written and when it's deployed
items.explanation: TOCTOU names the specific window — between checking a value and using it — where a second operation's read can slip in before the first operation's write lands.
items.reference:
TOCTOU
👀 Time of check
⚙️ ... gap ...
✍️ Time of use
Why: naming the gap is the first step to closing it.

TOCTOU

⚙️ ... gap ...
✍️ Time of use
Why: naming the gap is the first step to closing it.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, when does 'making it atomic' fit best?
choices: When the check and update touch a single resource and the datastore can express the condition directly
When the critical section spans multiple unrelated resources
When the operation must call an external payment API mid-operation
When performance doesn't matter at all
items.explanation: Atomic operations work best for a single-resource, single-step condition-and-update — like a conditional decrement — where the datastore itself can guarantee indivisibility.
items.reference:
Two strategies
🧱 Atomic — single resource, cheap
🔒 Lock — multi-step, more general
Why: picking the wrong one either overcomplicates a simple case or fails to cover a complex one.

items.explanation: Locks serialize access, which is more general but means waiting callers sit idle — atomic operations avoid that cost when they're available, since nothing has to wait.
items.reference:
Two strategies
🧱 Atomic — single resource, cheap
🔒 Lock — multi-step, more general
Why: picking the wrong one either overcomplicates a simple case or fails to cover a complex one.

items.prompt: Node.js is single-threaded — only one line of code runs at any instant. How does L3's racy code still produce a race condition?
choices: Because `await` is a yield point that hands control back to the event loop, letting another async call's code run before the first one resumes
Because Node.js actually runs multiple threads for async functions behind the scenes
Because the `delay` function forces the CPU to run two instructions simultaneously
It doesn't — the described race condition is not actually reproducible in Node.js
items.explanation: Single-threaded doesn't mean uninterleaved — every `await` yields control, and the event loop can run a different call's code during that yield, which is exactly how two concurrent async calls both see stock = 1.
items.reference:
Single-threaded ≠ no races
⏸️ await = yield point
🔀 Event loop can interleave here
Why: this is the mechanism that makes the bug real and reproducible, not theoretical.

items.prompt: In L3's `Mutex`, what happens when `acquire()` is called while the mutex is already locked?
choices: The resolver is pushed onto a queue instead of being resolved immediately, so the caller waits
An error is thrown immediately
The lock is forcibly released from whoever holds it
The call resolves immediately anyway, ignoring the lock
items.explanation: When already locked, `acquire()` pushes the resolve function onto `this.queue` rather than calling it, which is what makes the caller's promise stay pending until `release()` hands it the lock.
items.reference:
Mutex mechanics
🔓 Unlocked → resolve immediately
🔒 Locked → queue the resolver
Why: the queue is what makes waiters resolve in order, one at a time.

items.prompt: In L3's `Mutex.release()`, why does it hand the lock directly to the next queued waiter instead of just setting `locked = false`?
choices: Setting `locked = false` alone would let a brand-new `acquire()` call race with a waiter that's been queued longer, breaking the ordering guarantee
Handing it directly is required by JavaScript's syntax rules
It's purely a performance optimization with no correctness impact
There's no actual difference between the two approaches
items.explanation: If release() just unlocked and let any caller race for it, a queued waiter could be skipped by a fresh acquire() call — handing the lock directly to the next queued resolver preserves first-come, first-served ordering.
items.reference:
Mutex mechanics
🔓 Unlocked → resolve immediately
🔒 Locked → queue the resolver
Why: the queue is what makes waiters resolve in order, one at a time.

items.prompt: According to L3's failure modes, what's wrong with locking in application code while another process bypasses it?
choices: A lock only protects callers that acquire it — a second process writing directly to the same store isn't covered
Locking in application code is always slower than database-level locking
It's actually a complete fix with no remaining risk
It only matters if the second process is written in a different language
items.explanation: An in-process lock is a cooperative mechanism — it only protects code paths that actually call acquire() on it, so any writer that skips the lock entirely can still race with protected callers.
items.reference:
Failure modes
🔓 Locks only bind callers that use them
🐢 Holding a lock over slow work kills throughput
Why: both failure modes come from misunderstanding what a lock actually covers.

items.prompt: According to L3's failure modes, what's the risk of holding a lock across a slow, unrelated operation?

There's no risk — locks should always be held for as long as possible
It causes the lock to silently fail and stop protecting the critical section
It only affects readonly operations, never writes
items.explanation: A lock should wrap only the actual critical section — holding it across unrelated slow work forces unrelated callers to wait unnecessarily, which is a self-inflicted performance problem, not a correctness one.
items.reference:
Failure modes

🐢 Holding a lock over slow work kills throughput
Why: both failure modes come from misunderstanding what a lock actually covers.

Mutex mechanics
🔓 Unlocked → resolve immediately
🔒 Locked → queue the resolver
Why: the queue is what makes waiters resolve in order, one at a time.

items.prompt: Implement `Mutex.acquire()`, matching L3: it returns a `Promise`. If the mutex isn't locked, lock it (`this.locked = true`) and resolve immediately. If it's already locked, push the resolver onto `this.queue` instead of resolving yet, so the caller waits until `release()` hands it the lock.

tests.expr: (() => { const m = new Mutex(); m.acquire(); return expect(m.locked).toBe(true); })()

items.explanation: The Promise executor runs synchronously, so the locked check and either resolving or queueing happen as one atomic step from the caller's perspective — that's what prevents two concurrent acquire() calls from both seeing the mutex as unlocked.
